results.title: How to Set Up Google Cloud Run: 13 Steps, 80 Min [2026]
results.content:
As recently as July 11, 2026, Cloud Run’s pricing page still listed the Tier 1 request-based rate of $0.000024 per vCPU-second and $0.0000025 per GiB-second alongside the 2-million-free-requests-a-month allotment, according to Officebook.dev. That changed with the pricing page’s August 2026 refresh, which cut default request-based compute pricing to $0.000018 per vCPU-second and $0.000002 per GiB-second, plus $0.40 per million requests beyond the free allotment. The monthly free tier for request-based billing covers 2 million requests, 180,000 vCPU-seconds, and 360,000 GiB-seconds, which is generous enough that a lot of small APIs and internal tools never generate a bill at all. Instance-based billing now lines up with that same per-second rate ($0.000018 per vCPU-second, $0.000002 per GiB-second) but keeps its own separate free tier of 240,000 vCPU-seconds and 450,000 GiB-seconds per month (source: Cloud Run pricing).

| Billing mode | vCPU price | Memory price | Free tier (monthly) |
 ---  --- |
| Request-based (Tier 1) | $0.000024/vCPU-sec | $0.0000025/GiB-sec | 2M requests, 180,000 vCPU-sec, 360,000 GiB-sec |
| Instance-based | $0.000018/vCPU-sec | $0.000002/GiB-sec | 240,000 vCPU-sec, 450,000 GiB-sec |
| Requests (beyond free tier) | $0.40 per million requests | 2 million included |Put into a concrete example: a service handling 500,000 requests a month, each using 0.5 vCPU and 512 MB of memory for about 200 milliseconds, stays entirely inside the free tier. That’s roughly 50,000 vCPU-seconds and 50,000 GiB-seconds of usage, well under the 180,000 and 360,000 free allotments. Scale that same service to 5 million requests a month and the math changes: around 320,000 billable vCPU-seconds ($7.68), 140,000 billable GiB-seconds ($0.35), and 3 million billable requests ($1.20), for a total of roughly $9.23 a month. For comparison, AWS Lambda’s always-free monthly tier covers 1,000,000 requests and 400,000 GB-seconds (source: AWS Lambda pricing), a smaller request allowance than Cloud Run’s but a comparable compute allotment, so the two are closer in practice than the headline numbers suggest.

### Choosing Between Request-Based and Instance-Based Billing

Default to request-based billing unless you have a specific reason not to. It’s cheaper for the overwhelming majority of web APIs, since most requests spend a fraction of a second doing actual CPU work and the rest waiting on a database or an upstream call, and Cloud Run doesn’t charge for that waiting time under request-based billing. Switch to instance-based billing only when your service genuinely needs CPU available outside the request-response cycle: a WebSocket server holding open connections, a background worker pulling from a queue, or anything running a timer or a cache-warming routine between requests. Picking instance-based billing for a plain REST API is the single easiest way to overpay for Cloud Run, since you’d be paying for CPU the container isn’t using.

## Step 1: Install and Initialize the Google Cloud CLI

Everything in this tutorial runs through `gcloud`, the command-line interface for Google Cloud. Install the latest release for your platform (source: Google Cloud CLI install guide), then authenticate and confirm the install:

```
curl  | bash exec -l $SHELL gcloud init gcloud auth login gcloud version
``` [...] ## Frequently Asked Questions

### Is Google Cloud Run free?

For low-traffic services, effectively yes. The monthly free tier covers 2 million requests, 180,000 vCPU-seconds, and 360,000 GiB-seconds under request-based billing (source: Cloud Run pricing). Past that, you pay per-second for exactly what your container uses.

### What’s the difference between Cloud Run services and Cloud Run functions?

Services deploy a full container image you build yourself and can hold traffic indefinitely or scale to zero between requests. Cloud Run functions is the lighter, source-based deployment model (the evolution of Cloud Functions), billed by memory and vCPU allocation per 100 milliseconds, with a maximum allocation of 32,768 MB and 8 vCPU on the largest tier.

### Does Cloud Run support GPUs?

Yes, Cloud Run supports NVIDIA L4 GPUs for services that need accelerated inference, which lets teams serve AI models on the same serverless container model covered in this tutorial instead of provisioning a dedicated GKE cluster.

### What programming languages does Cloud Run support?

Any language or runtime that can be packaged into a container. Cloud Run runs standard container images directly rather than restricting deployments to a fixed list of managed language runtimes, which is the core difference from function-as-a-service platforms. Even the managed-runtime side keeps pace, though: Google added Python 3.13 support on April 21, 2025, bringing the number of supported Python runtime versions for Cloud Run functions up to four.

### How does Cloud Run pricing compare to AWS Lambda?

Cloud Run’s request-based free tier covers 2 million requests, 180,000 vCPU-seconds, and 360,000 GiB-seconds a month. Lambda’s always-free tier covers 1,000,000 requests and 400,000 GB-seconds a month (source: AWS Lambda pricing). Cloud Run’s request allowance is larger, Lambda’s compute allowance is comparable, and the bigger practical difference is that Cloud Run runs any container while Lambda expects code in a supported runtime.

### Can Cloud Run connect to a database?

Yes. For Cloud SQL, the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy pattern or a Serverless VPC Access connector are the two common paths, letting a Cloud Run service reach a private database instance without exposing it publicly.

### Does Cloud Run scale to zero?

Yes, when `min-instances` is left at its default of 0. An idle service costs nothing beyond the image storage sitting in Artifact Registry until the next request arrives and a new instance starts.

### How many concurrent requests can one Cloud Run instance handle?

80 by default, configurable up to a maximum of 1,000 per instance (source: Cloud Run concurrency documentation). The right number depends on whether your workload is CPU-bound or mostly waiting on I/O like database calls.Getting a container onto Cloud Run takes maybe twenty minutes. Getting it production-ready, tuned concurrency, secrets pulled from Secret Manager instead of hardcoded, a custom domain with managed TLS, and deploys that happen automatically on every push, is the rest of this guide. Start with Step 1’s CLI setup, keep the image slim from Step 6 onward, and the defaults Google ships will carry you further than most tutorials give them credit for.

results.content:
### Focus

Cloud Run allows you to run code either as a continous service that responds to web requests and events, or as a job that exits when finished. Both operate within the same environment and can use the same integrations. You can write code using your favorite language, framework, and libraries, package it up as a container, run `gcloud run deploy` and your app will be live. Or, you can directly deploy from source and let Cloud Run handle containerizing your code with buildpacks . Cloud Run partly mitigates vendor lock-in with standard OCI container images, a declarative API model and resources that can be represented in YAML files.

### Key Features

Cloud Run can access most major Google Cloud services using language-specific API client libraries and/or REST APIs, including Cloud CDN for Edge computing. Microservices deployed in Cloud Run scale automatically based on the number of incoming requests.

An extensive overview of the quotas and limits can be found in the Cloud Run Resources.

Based on resource consumption during execution beyond the free tier, with billing rounded up to the nearest 100 milliseconds.\ \\ More details here.Requests: $0.40 per million

\Note the mixed use of GiB and GB. Prices are listed for Services in Tier 1 regions and may vary by region.

# Google Cloud Pricing Models and Examples for 11 Services 

Google Cloud offers a free tier with a $300 credit; pricing models range from pay-as-you-go to committed use discounts and Spot VMs.

FWT

Finout Writing Team

Apr 30th, 2026  19 min read

URL Copied

![Google Cloud Pricing Models and Examples for 11 Services ](

Table of Contents

## How Does Google Cloud Price Its Services?

Google Cloud uses a consumption-based pricing model that allows organizations to pay only for the resources they use. This flexibility is paired with multiple pricing options designed to support different workload types and usage patterns. With the pay-as-you-go model, users are charged per unit of resource—such as CPU time, memory, or storage—with billing typically calculated by the second or minute. This model suits dynamic workloads that vary in usage.For more predictable workloads, Google Cloud offers Committed Use Discounts (CUDs). These allow users to commit to using specific resources (e.g., vCPUs, RAM) over a one- or three-year term in exchange for reduced rates—often yielding significant savings. Another built-in savings mechanism is Sustained Use Discounts (SUDs). These apply automatically when eligible services, like Compute Engine, run for a large portion of a billing cycle, providing up to 30% off without a commitment.

To support cost-sensitive or fault-tolerant applications, Google Cloud provides Spot VM Instances—heavily discounted virtual machines using surplus capacity. While cost-effective, these instances can be preempted at any time. For enterprises with large or unique workloads, custom discounts and pricing agreements are available through sales negotiation. This can include volume-based discounts or tailored billing structures.

This is part of an extensive series of guides about FinOps.

  

## What is the Google Cloud Free Tier?

Google Cloud has a simple offer to get you started: a $300 spend-it-as-you-like credit. This offer expands if you share and verify a business email address.

This approach seems less generous than AWS' and Azure's, which offer free tier services for up to 12 months to new customers. However, Google Cloud combines its new customer treats with an "always free" usage threshold for certain services (as detailed here). Google Cloud also offers over 20 products that are free up to designated monthly thresholds.

## Google Cloud Pricing Models [...] ## Google Cloud Services Pricing with Examples

It is not the intention of this article to give you an overview of every service offered by Google Cloud or the Google Cloud Marketplace; rather, we will discuss the more popular service offerings and how they are priced.

### 1. Compute Engine

Google Cloud’s Compute Engine is part of its IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service), equivalent to AWS’ EC2 service. Google Cloud takes its pay-for-what-you-use very seriously, with all vCPUs, GPUs, and GB of memory charged in per-second increments, with a 60-second minimum.

You can opt for either of the models discussed above: pay-as-you-go or committed use. The Google Cloud even rewards the pay-as-you-go user with sustained use discounts. Even if you don’t commit and apply the committed use model, there are discounts of up to 30% for running specific Compute Engine resources for a significant portion of a billing cycle.

Pricing example:

If you run an e2-standard-2 virtual machine (2 vCPUs, 8 GB memory) in the Iowa (us-central1) region:

 Pay-as-you-go rate: approx. $0.067 per hour
 Monthly total (730 hours): ~$48.91
 Sustained use discount: Applied automatically for long-running instances
 Committed use discount (1-year): Can reduce cost by up to 27%, bringing the monthly cost down to around $35.70

These prices exclude any additional costs like network egress, premium images, or attached disks.

### 2. Google Kubernetes Engine(GKE)
